sections.b: Micah 5:2 names Bethlehem, a village too small to count among the clans of Judah, as the place the LORD will bring out a ruler for Israel, 'for me'. Its older name Ephrathah ties it to Rachel's grave (Genesis 35:19), to David's father (1 Samuel 17:12) and to Boaz (Ruth 4:11). Matthew 2:5-6 quotes the verse with changes, and John 7:42 shows the expectation in Jesus' day. The verse is the Bible's chief statement of why a village matters.
sections.refs: Micah 5:2; Matthew 2:5-6; John 7:42; Genesis 35:19; 1 Samuel 17:12; Ruth 4:11

common: Micah 5:2 expects a Davidic ruler, from David's home town.
uncommon: Some critical readers see the ruler as a king of the 8th or 6th century, not a future messiah.

sections.b: Micah 5:2-5 promises a ruler whose origins 'reach back to the distant past', who shepherds by the LORD's strength and whose greatness reaches the ends of the earth. Jewish tradition reads it of the Messiah (Targum Jonathan, Rashi). Matthew 2:4-6 asks 'Where will the Messiah be born?' and answers with this verse. Whether Micah meant a particular king (Hezekiah, a later Davidide) or an end-time figure is debated; the Plain English Translation keeps the text open.

common: Jews and Christians have both read Micah 5:2 of the Messiah.
uncommon: Some scholars read it only of an 8th-century king.

sections.h: A king from David's own beginnings
sections.b: Micah 5:2 goes back behind Jerusalem's court to the village from which David came. The promise made in 2 Samuel 7 (a house, a throne forever) is not dropped, but its next king is looked for where David started, among the shepherds. The phrase 'to be ruler over Israel' echoes the LORD's words to David (2 Samuel 5:2; 7:8).

sections.h: The remnant of Jacob as dew and as a lion
sections.b: Micah 5:7-8 gives the remnant two images: dew from the LORD that needs no human help, and a lion among sheep. The remnant is the small group left after judgment (2:12; 4:7), a source of blessing to the nations and a danger to oppressors. Micah 7:18 ends the book by saying the LORD forgives the rebellion of 'the remnant of his inheritance'.
sections.refs: Micah 5:7; Micah 5:8; Micah 7:18; Micah 2:12; Micah 4:7; Romans 9:27

sections.h: The shepherd king and the shepherd God in Micah
sections.b: Micah uses shepherd for a ruler (5:4), for a team of leaders who defeat Assyria (5:5-6) and for the LORD himself, asked to shepherd his people with his rod (7:14). The three belong together: the human shepherd stands 'in the strength of the LORD', and the prayer asks the LORD to do what no human shepherd did.
sections.refs: Micah 5:4; Micah 5:5; Micah 5:6; Micah 7:14; 2 Samuel 5:2; Ezekiel 34:23; Psalm 28:9

sections.h: Assyria and the land of Nimrod
sections.b: Micah 5:5-6 expects Assyria to invade and to be answered by seven shepherds and eight leaders of men; the land of Assyria will be shepherded 'with the sword' and 'the land of Nimrod' at its gates. Micah 7:12 lists Assyria first among the places from which people come to the rebuilt city. Whether 'Assyria' means the Assyria of 701 BC, or later empires, is debated.

Micah prophesied 'in the days of Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah' (1:1). Chapter 5 fits Sennacherib's siege in 701 BC (5:1), and some read the ruler of 5:2 as Hezekiah or his heir. The elders in Jeremiah 26:18-19 remembered that Hezekiah did not kill Micah but feared the LORD and begged for mercy. The cleansing of 5:12-14 matches what Hezekiah did in 2 Kings 18:4.
sections.refs: Micah 5:1; Micah 5:13; Micah 5:14; Jeremiah 26:18; 2 Kings 18:4; 2 Kings 18:13

sections.h: The woman in labor in Micah 5:3 and Isaiah 7:14
sections.b: Micah 5:3 says the LORD will hand his people over 'until the time a woman in labor gives birth'. Isaiah 7:14 has a young woman pregnant with a son named Immanuel. Both are from the same generation of prophets (Micah 1:1; Isaiah 1:1). Whether one verse depends on the other is not provable; Matthew's gospel joins the two promises to Jesus' birth (Matthew 1:22-23; 2:5-6).
Micah 5:12 puts 'sorceries' and 'sign-readers' among the false supports the LORD will cut away. The same two practices are in Deuteronomy 18:10 and, for Manasseh, in 2 Kings 21:6.
Micah 5:13 includes 'standing stones' with 'carved images' that the LORD will cut away from Judah. Hezekiah smashed such stones (2 Kings 18:4), and Deuteronomy 16:22 forbade them.
Micah 5:14 says the LORD will pull up Judah's Asherah poles and demolish her cities. Hezekiah cut down an Asherah pole (2 Kings 18:4); Ahab made one in Samaria (1 Kings 16:33).

sections.h: A day that cleans out the land
sections.b: In Micah 5:10-15 'that day' is a day on which the LORD removes his own people's horses, chariots, fortresses, magic and idols, and takes vengeance on nations that did not listen. It is a day of the LORD that purifies before it rescues.

Micah 6:5 asks Israel to remember what Balak planned and what Balaam answered. Balaam's answer was a blessing, not the curse Balak paid for. Later tradition remembers him also for his advice at Peor (Numbers 31:16).
Micah 6:5 mentions Shittim and Gilgal together: the last camp east of the Jordan and the first camp west of it. The phrase takes the people from the edge of the land across the river.
Micah 6:4 says the LORD sent Moses, Aaron and Miriam ahead of Israel. It is the only place in the prophets that names her as one of the leaders sent by God.

sections.h: The Exodus at the start, middle and end of Micah 6-7
sections.b: Micah 6:4 opens the lawsuit with the Exodus; 7:15 promises 'wonders' as in the days of the Exodus; 7:19 throws sins into the 'depths' where Egypt's army sank (Exodus 15:5). The new Exodus is the pattern of the book's hope.

sections.h: What the worshipper asks in Micah 6:6-8
sections.b: Micah 6:6-7 asks how much to bring: calves, thousands of rams, rivers of oil, a firstborn child. The answer in 6:8 is not 'no sacrifice' but 'do justice, love loyal love, and walk in humility'. Isaiah 1:11-17, Amos 5:21-24 and Hosea 6:6 say the same.
sections.refs: Micah 6:6; Micah 6:7; Micah 6:8; Isaiah 1:11; Amos 5:21; Hosea 6:6

common: The prophets reject sacrifice without justice, not sacrifice itself.
uncommon: Some critical scholars read the prophets as rejecting the whole sacrificial system.

sections.b: The worshipper of Micah 6:7 asks if the LORD wants his firstborn for his rebellion. Ahaz, in Micah's days, 'made his son pass through the fire' (2 Kings 16:3); the law forbids it (Leviticus 18:21), and Jeremiah has the LORD say he never commanded it (Jeremiah 7:31).

sections.h: Micah 6:8 and the justice of Micah 6-7
sections.b: Micah 6:8 says what the LORD asks: to do justice (mishpat), to love loyal love (hesed) and to walk with your God in humility. Micah 6:10-12 names false measures and violence as the opposite; 7:3 names the corrupt judge; 7:9 trusts the LORD to do the speaker justice. The Talmud (Makkot 24a) says Micah reduced 613 commandments to three.
sections.refs: Micah 6:8; Micah 6:10; Micah 6:11; Micah 7:3; Micah 7:9; Matthew 23:23

sections.b: Micah asks people to 'love loyal love' (6:8), says the loyal person has vanished (7:2) and ends by saying the LORD delights in loyal love (7:18) and will show it to Abraham (7:20). The same word is asked of people and given by God.

sections.h: The rules of Omri in Micah 6:16
sections.b: Micah 6:16 charges the city with keeping the rules of Omri and the works of the house of Ahab. Omri built Samaria; Ahab took Naboth's vineyard (1 Kings 21). The charge links Micah's accusation of land-grabbing (2:1-2) to the northern dynasty.
Micah 6:14-15 gives the curses of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28: eating without being filled, sowing without reaping, pressing olives without anointing, making wine without drinking it.

Micah 7:1 pictures a gleaner who comes after the harvest and finds nothing. The poor lived by gleaning (Leviticus 19:9-10). The image is of a land with no loyal person left, and it follows chapters 2-3 where the powerful take the poor's fields and judges take bribes.
Micah 7:4 speaks of 'the day your watchmen spoke of'. In the prophets 'watchman' often means the prophet who warns (Ezekiel 3:17; Jeremiah 6:17).
Micah 7:1-6 is a personal lament over a land with no loyal person in it. It resembles Psalm 12 and Jeremiah 9, and turns at 7:7 to trust.
Jesus takes Micah 7:6, a description of a land that has lost its trust, and applies it to what happens in households when people follow him (Matthew 10:35-36; Luke 12:53).

sections.h: The enemy who says 'Where is your God?'
sections.b: Micah 7:8-10 speaks of an enemy (a feminine word) who gloats over the speaker and will be trampled like mud. Babylon, Edom and other powers have been proposed; the text names none.

sections.h: A day for building the walls
sections.b: Micah 7:11 promises a day for building the walls of the city and for pushing out its boundary; 5:1 shows the same city under siege. The rebuilding of the walls is read as Nehemiah's work or as a future restoration.
Micah 7:12-17 shows people coming from Assyria, Egypt, the River, the sea and the mountains, and nations that lick the dust and come in dread to the LORD. Compare Micah 4:1-4.

sections.h: 'Who is a God like you?' and the name Micah
sections.b: The prophet's name (Mikhah in 1:1, Mikhayah in the written text of Jeremiah 26:18) means 'Who is like Yah?'. Micah 7:18 asks mi El kamokha, 'Who is a God like you?', and answers by listing what the LORD does: forgive, pass over rebellion, delight in loyal love. The question echoes Exodus 15:11.

sections.h: 'You will throw all their sins into the depths of the sea'
sections.b: Micah 7:18-20 is the Twelve's fullest statement of God's forgiveness: he forgives guilt, passes over rebellion, does not keep his anger, subdues guilt and throws sin into the sea, and keeps the oath to Abraham. It is read on Shabbat Shuvah and at tashlich in Jewish practice, and in Lent in the Roman lectionary.

common: God's forgiveness in Micah 7:18-20 rests on the Exodus creed.

sections.h: Micah's closing creed and its neighbors
sections.b: Micah 7:18-20 uses Exodus 34:6-7, as Joel 2:13, Jonah 4:2 and Nahum 1:3 do. Micah keeps the forgiving half, Nahum the half about the guilty. Micah 7:10 and Joel 2:17 share the question 'Where is your God?'.
sections.refs: Micah 7:18; Joel 2:13; Jonah 4:2; Nahum 1:2; Micah 7:10; Joel 2:17

sections.h: The oath to Abraham in Micah 7:20
sections.b: Micah 7:20 ends the book with the oath the LORD swore to Abraham and Jacob: faithfulness and loyal love. The promise to the fathers is the ground for the forgiveness of 7:18-19.

Micah 6:1-8 is the prophets' clearest courtroom scene: the LORD brings a case before the mountains and hills and asks his people to testify against him. It states his benefits (the Exodus, the leaders, Balaam) and the worshipper's question about offerings, and answers with the three things in 6:8.
